steps.title: Init Memory Gauge
text: Set up the memory gauge between players.
Set the memory gauge between both players with the marker starting at 0 in the center. The left side is your memory, the right side is your opponent's. Memory can never exceed 10.

steps.title: Shuffle & Place Decks
text: Shuffle your main deck and Digi-Egg deck, then place both face-down on the field.
Thoroughly randomize both your main deck and your Digi-Egg deck.
Give your opponent the opportunity to shuffle or cut your decks after you're done.
Place your main deck face-down in the deck area, and your Digi-Egg deck face-down in its designated area. Neither player may look at or change the order of cards in either deck.

steps.title: Determine First Player
text: Play Rock-Paper-Scissors; the winner chooses who goes first.
Both players play Rock-Paper-Scissors. The winner freely decides whether to go first or second — no outside intervention is allowed.

steps.title: Draw Opening Hand
text: Each player draws 5 cards from their deck as their starting hand.
Both players draw the top 5 cards of their deck. This is your initial hand — keep it secret from your opponent.
You may freely look at and rearrange the cards in your own hand at any time.

steps.title: Mulligan (Optional)
text: Each player may redraw their entire hand once, starting with the first player.
Starting with the first player, each player may declare a re-draw. If you do, return all cards from your hand to your deck, reshuffle, and draw a new hand of 5 cards.
You can only do this once — after taking your mulligan (or choosing not to), you must keep that hand.
Tip: If your opening hand has no low-level Digimon or no rookies to hatch, strongly consider taking the mulligan.

steps.title: Place Security Stack
text: Take the top 5 cards off your deck and place them face-down, one at a time, as your security.
Take 5 cards from the top of your deck and place them face-down one at a time without looking at their faces. The card at the top of your deck ends up at the bottom of your security stack.
Spread the security cards out so the number of cards can be seen by both players. You cannot change the order of cards in your security stack.
When your opponent attacks you directly, the top card of your security stack is checked. If it has a [Security] effect, you may activate it.

steps.title: Deck — Main Deck
text: Exactly 50 cards made up of Digimon, Tamer, and Option cards.
You can include up to 4 copies of the same card (by card number).

steps.title: Deck — Digi-Egg Deck
text: 0 to 5 cards. As long as it has 5 or fewer cards, it can have as many cards as you like, or even be empty.
Can include up to 4 copies of a card with the same card number.
Your play area is arranged as shown above. Cards are either Unsuspended (vertical) or Suspended (horizontal). When paying costs or attacking, you suspend cards.
**The Game Areas**
bullets: **① Deck** — Your 50-card draw pile, face-down. A private area — neither player can look at or change its order.
**② Digi-Egg Deck** — 0–5 card deck, face-down. A private area where your egg cards wait to be hatched.
**③ Breeding Area** — Where hatched Digimon go. Max 1 card. Cards here are protected from nearly all effects.
**④ Battle Area** — Your main play zone. Any number of cards can be here. Digimon, Tamers, and Option cards all go here when played.
**⑤ Trash** — Discard pile, face-up. A public area — both players can look through it at any time.
**⑥ Security Stack** — 5 face-down cards from the start of the game. When attacked directly, the top security card is checked.
**⑦ Hand** — Your cards held in secret. You may freely rearrange them.

text: **The Memory Gauge**
Memory is the shared resource used to pay costs. 0 is the center. Numbers on your left are your memory; numbers on your right are your opponent's memory. Memory never exceeds 10.
When you pay a cost, move the marker right toward your opponent. When you "gain memory," move it left toward you. Loss of memory moves it right.
Your turn ends when the memory reaches 1 or more on your opponent's side. The more you do on your turn, the more memory you give your opponent for their turn.
